title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

reading.body:
This is a synthetic-media impersonation failure, in which fabricated video and audio are made to appear as the output of a real news organisation. The fake Mother Jones video carries a false claim about a payment to a named broadcaster, and it uses a forged version of the outlet's logo and manipulated footage of its editor-in-chief. The impersonation sits at the distribution layer rather than inside any single platform's model: the material was posted to social media accounts, and the outlet's complaint led one platform to remove a post under its trademark policy.

Catching this kind of operation requires verifying the claimed source rather than the content alone. A reader or platform would need to confirm that Mother Jones published the video, that the logo and the footage of its editor were authentic, and that the payment described had occurred. The reporting notes that researchers identified bot-like behaviour in the accounts and judged the view counts likely inflated, which means the apparent reach of the posts is not a reliable measure of how many people actually saw them.

The facts do not establish who produced the videos, whether the accounts were directed by a state, or what effect the campaign had on voters. The attribution to a named network and the description of the operation as a Russian influence effort are the reporting's characterisation, not a finding in this record.

reports.title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

summary:
A Russian disinformation network called Matryoshka, also known as Storm-1679, has been circulating a fake Mother Jones video on social media. The video falsely claims the Democratic National Committee paid $259 million to CNN chief Mark Thompson to promote gender transition among children, and it uses a fake Mother Jones logo and doctored footage of editor-in-chief Clara Jeffery. It drew about 155,000 views on one X account and 50,000 on another. Researchers say the accounts show bot-like signs and the view counts were likely inflated.

The campaign also includes deepfakes of celebrities such as Sarah Jessica Parker, Julia Roberts, and Christopher Lloyd urging votes for Republicans, plus fake CNN and other news reports about Democratic candidates. Mother Jones complained to X, which removed one post for violating its trademark policy. The article says the operation has not yet gone viral, but it warns that Russian influence efforts will continue ahead of the midterms, especially since the Trump administration has closed government units that once tracked foreign disinformation.
